name: composite
summary: Ops assembled from the primitives rather than from a kernel.
extended:
118 functions defined in `lucid/_ops/composite/` — the aliases (`absolute`, `arctan2`, ...), the fused arithmetic helpers (`addmm`, `addcdiv`, ...), and the statistical and linear-algebra conveniences.

They carry no kernel and no backward of their own: gradients fall out of the primitives they are written in.  That makes them cheap to add and correct by construction, at the cost of materialising the intermediates a fused kernel would not.

members.name: absolute
members.summary: Element-wise absolute value.
members.extended:
Verbose alias of `lucid.abs`, exposed for parity with reference
frameworks that publish both `abs` and `absolute` spellings of the
same operation.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor. Any numeric dtype.

returns.description:
Tensor of the same shape and dtype as `input` containing
$|x_i|$ element-wise.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([-1.5, 0.0, 2.0])
>>> lucid.absolute(x)
tensor([1.5, 0., 2.])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out}_i = |x_i|
$$

The gradient is $\operatorname{sign}(x_i)$; the sub-gradient at
$x_i = 0$ is conventionally taken to be `0`.

members.name: acosh
members.summary: Inverse hyperbolic cosine.
members.extended:
Short-name alias of `arccosh`. Computes the principal branch of
$\operatorname{arccosh}(x)$ for real inputs.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor with values in the domain $x \geq 1$.

returns.description: Element-wise inverse hyperbolic cosine.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 10.0])
>>> lucid.acosh(x)
tensor([0., 1.317, 2.993])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\operatorname{acosh}(x) = \log\!\bigl(x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\bigr),
\qquad x \geq 1.
$$

Inputs with $x < 1$ produce NaN. The derivative is
$1 / \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}$, which is singular at $x = 1$.

members.name: addbmm
members.signature: addbmm(input: Tensor, batch1: Tensor, batch2: Tensor, beta: _float = ..., alpha: _float = ...)
members.summary: Batched matmul with reduction over the batch axis.
members.extended:
Computes
$\beta \cdot \text{input} + \alpha \cdot \sum_{k} (\text{batch1}[k] \cdot \text{batch2}[k])$.
Useful for accumulating multiple parallel matrix products into a
single output matrix (e.g. summing per-head attention contributions).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Accumulator of shape `(M, N)`.

parameters.name: batch1
parameters.description: Batched left matrices of shape `(B, M, K)`.

parameters.name: batch2
parameters.description: Batched right matrices of shape `(B, K, N)`.

parameters.name: beta
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `input`. Defaults to `1.0`.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on the batched matmul sum. Defaults to `1.0`.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(M, N)`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> b1 = lucid.ones((3, 2, 4))
>>> b2 = lucid.ones((3, 4, 2))
>>> M = lucid.zeros((2, 2))
>>> lucid.addbmm(M, b1, b2)
tensor([[12., 12.], [12., 12.]])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out} = \beta \cdot \text{input}
+ \alpha \sum_{k = 0}^{B - 1}
(\text{batch1}[k] \cdot \text{batch2}[k]).
$$

Differs from `baddbmm` in that the batch dimension is reduced
away; `baddbmm` keeps the per-batch results.

members.name: addcdiv
members.signature: addcdiv(input: Tensor, tensor1: Tensor, tensor2: Tensor, value: _float = ...)
members.summary: Element-wise fused divide-add.
members.extended:
Computes $\text{input} + \text{value} \cdot (t_1 / t_2)$ in
one expression. Common in optimiser updates (e.g. Adam's
parameter step uses the form `param -= lr * m / sqrt(v)`).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Accumulator tensor.

parameters.name: tensor1
parameters.description: Numerator. Must broadcast with `input` and `tensor2`.

parameters.name: tensor2
parameters.description: Denominator. Must broadcast with `input` and `tensor1`.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on the quotient. Defaults to `1`.

returns.description: Tensor with the broadcast shape of the inputs.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> a = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0])
>>> t1 = lucid.tensor([4.0, 9.0])
>>> t2 = lucid.tensor([2.0, 3.0])
>>> lucid.addcdiv(a, t1, t2, value=0.5)
tensor([2., 3.5])
notes:
Element-wise definition:



$$
\text{out}_i = \text{input}_i
+ \text{value} \cdot \frac{(t_1)_i}{(t_2)_i}.
$$

Division by zero follows standard IEEE 754 rules — no clamping is
applied. Gradients flow through all three tensor operands.

members.name: addcmul
members.signature: addcmul(input: Tensor, tensor1: Tensor, tensor2: Tensor, value: _float = ...)
members.summary: Element-wise fused multiply-add with a scalar weight.
members.extended:
Computes $\text{input} + \text{value} \cdot (t_1 \odot t_2)$
element-wise, where $\odot$ denotes the Hadamard (element-wise)
product.  Provided as a single named op for readability and to give
the dispatcher the chance to fuse the three steps into one kernel on
backends that support it.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Tensor that is added to the scaled element-wise product.

parameters.name: tensor1
parameters.description:
Left operand of the element-wise product.  Must broadcast with
`input` and `tensor2`.

parameters.name: tensor2
parameters.description:
Right operand of the element-wise product.  Must broadcast with
`input` and `tensor1`.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description:
Scalar multiplier applied to the product `t1 * t2` before
addition.  Defaults to `1` (plain multiply-and-add).

returns.description:
Element-wise result with the broadcast shape of the three input
tensors.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> a = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
>>> b = lucid.tensor([4.0, 5.0, 6.0])
>>> c = lucid.tensor([0.5, 0.5, 0.5])
>>> lucid.addcmul(a, b, c, value=2.0)
tensor([5., 7., 9.])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out}_i =
\text{input}_i + \text{value} \cdot (t_{1,i} \cdot t_{2,i}).
$$

Sister op of `addcdiv` (`input + value * t1 / t2`).  Common
in optimisers (e.g. running-mean / running-variance updates) where a
bias-correction term is added to an existing accumulator.

members.name: addmm
members.signature: addmm(input: Tensor, mat1: Tensor, mat2: Tensor, beta: _float = ..., alpha: _float = ...)
members.summary: General matrix multiply with a scaled accumulator (GEMM).
members.extended:
Computes $\beta \cdot \text{input} + \alpha \cdot (\text{mat1} \times \text{mat2})$,
the canonical BLAS-3 `gemm` operation. Useful for fused linear
layers: an output bias plus a weight multiplication in one call.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Accumulator of shape `(M, N)` (or broadcastable to it).

parameters.name: mat1
parameters.description: Left matrix of shape `(M, K)`.

parameters.name: mat2
parameters.description: Right matrix of shape `(K, N)`.

parameters.name: beta
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `input`. Defaults to `1.0`.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `mat1 @ mat2`. Defaults to `1.0`.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(M, N)`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> M = lucid.zeros((2, 2))
>>> a = lucid.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
>>> b = lucid.tensor([[5., 6.], [7., 8.]])
>>> lucid.addmm(M, a, b, beta=0.0, alpha=1.0)
tensor([[19., 22.], [43., 50.]])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out} = \beta \cdot \text{input}
+ \alpha \cdot (\text{mat1} \cdot \text{mat2}).
$$

The inner dimension `K` must match between `mat1` and `mat2`.
Standard dtype promotion applies; the matmul itself uses Accelerate
(CPU stream) or MLX (GPU stream).

members.name: addmv
members.signature: addmv(input: Tensor, mat: Tensor, vec: Tensor, beta: _float = ..., alpha: _float = ...)
members.summary: Matrix-vector multiply with a scaled accumulator (BLAS-2 gemv).
members.extended:
Computes
$\beta \cdot \text{input} + \alpha \cdot (\text{mat} \cdot \text{vec})$,
the canonical BLAS-2 `gemv` operation.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Accumulator vector of shape `(M,)`.

parameters.name: mat
parameters.description: Matrix of shape `(M, N)`.

parameters.name: vec
parameters.description: Vector of shape `(N,)`.

parameters.name: beta
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `input`. Defaults to `1.0`.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `mat @ vec`. Defaults to `1.0`.

returns.description: Vector of shape `(M,)`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> M = lucid.zeros(2)
>>> A = lucid.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
>>> v = lucid.tensor([5., 6.])
>>> lucid.addmv(M, A, v)
tensor([17., 39.])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out}_i = \beta \cdot \text{input}_i
+ \alpha \cdot \sum_{j = 0}^{N - 1} \text{mat}_{ij} \cdot \text{vec}_j.
$$

Implemented by promoting `vec` to a column `(N, 1)`, calling
`lucid.matmul`, and squeezing the trailing axis.

members.name: addr
members.signature: addr(input: Tensor, vec1: Tensor, vec2: Tensor, beta: _float = ..., alpha: _float = ...)
members.summary: Rank-1 update of a matrix by an outer product (BLAS-2 ger).
members.extended:
Computes
$\beta \cdot \text{input} + \alpha \cdot (\text{vec1} \otimes \text{vec2})$,
i.e. updates the matrix `input` by adding the (scaled) outer product
of two vectors. The classical BLAS `ger` routine.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Accumulator matrix of shape `(M, N)`.

parameters.name: vec1
parameters.description: First vector of length `M`.

parameters.name: vec2
parameters.description: Second vector of length `N`.

parameters.name: beta
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `input`. Defaults to `1.0`.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on the outer product. Defaults to `1.0`.

returns.description: Updated matrix of shape `(M, N)`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> M = lucid.zeros((2, 3))
>>> u = lucid.tensor([1., 2.])
>>> v = lucid.tensor([3., 4., 5.])
>>> lucid.addr(M, u, v)
tensor([[3., 4., 5.], [6., 8., 10.]])
notes:
Element-wise:



$$
\text{out}_{ij} = \beta \cdot \text{input}_{ij}
+ \alpha \cdot \text{vec1}_i \cdot \text{vec2}_j.
$$

The outer product is a rank-1 matrix, so this update can be used to
build rank-1 corrections in optimisation algorithms (Broyden / BFGS).

members.name: adjoint
members.summary: Conjugate (Hermitian) transpose of the trailing two dimensions.
members.extended:
For real-valued tensors this is identical to a plain transpose of the
last two axes. For complex tensors the entries are also conjugated,
yielding the Hermitian transpose $A^{*} = \overline{A^{T}}$.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor with at least 2 dimensions.

returns.description:
Tensor with the last two axes swapped (and complex conjugated
when applicable).

raises.description: If `x.ndim < 2`.

notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\mathbf{A}^{*} = \overline{\mathbf{A}^{T}}.
$$

For real inputs the conjugation step is a no-op, so this is simply
a permutation of the last two axes. Batch dimensions are preserved.

members.name: allclose
members.signature: allclose(input: Tensor, other: Tensor, rtol: _float = ..., atol: _float = ..., equal_nan: _bool = ...)
members.summary: Return `True` iff every element pair is close within tolerance.
members.extended:
Closeness predicate:

$$
|\text{input}_i - \text{other}_i| \le \text{atol}
    + \text{rtol} \cdot |\text{other}_i|.
$$

Note the asymmetry — the relative term uses `|other|`, so swapping
arguments can change the answer for marginal cases.  This matches
the NumPy / reference-framework convention.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Inputs to compare.  Must be broadcastable.

parameters.name: other
parameters.description: Inputs to compare.  Must be broadcastable.

parameters.name: rtol
parameters.description: Relative tolerance.  Default `1e-5`.

parameters.name: atol
parameters.description:
Absolute tolerance — dominates the bound when `|other|` is small
(think of comparisons near zero).  Default `1e-8`.

parameters.name: equal_nan
parameters.description:
When `True`, `NaN` positions are treated as equal to other
`NaN` positions.  Default `False` (any `NaN` makes the
predicate `False`).

returns.description:
Reduces to a single Python `bool` — synchronises any pending
GPU work to evaluate the final reduction.

see_also.name: isclose
see_also.description: element-wise variant that returns a Tensor of bools.

members.name: amax
members.signature: amax(input: Tensor, dim: _int | Sequence[_int] | None = ..., keepdim: _bool = ...)
members.summary: Reduce `input` to per-slice maxima along `dim` — values only.
members.extended:
Multi-axis sibling of `lucid.max` that returns *only* the
reduced values (never the indices) and accepts a tuple of axes
for a single fused reduction.  Use when you don't need the
`(values, indices)` tuple `lucid.max` returns.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.annotation: int, sequence of int, or None
parameters.description:
Axis or axes to reduce.  `None` (default) reduces over every
axis and returns a 0-D scalar tensor.

parameters.name: keepdim
parameters.description:
Retain the reduced axes as size-1 dimensions.  Default
`False`.

returns.description: Maxima along `dim`; shape depends on `dim` and `keepdim`.

see_also.name: lucid.max
see_also.description: returns `(values, indices)` for a single axis.

members.name: amin
members.signature: amin(input: Tensor, dim: _int | Sequence[_int] | None = ..., keepdim: _bool = ...)
members.summary: Reduce `input` to per-slice minima along `dim` — values only.
members.extended:
Mirror image of `amax`.  Accepts a tuple of axes for a fused
multi-axis reduction; returns just the minimum values (never the
indices).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.annotation: int, sequence of int, or None
parameters.description:
Axis or axes to reduce.  `None` (default) reduces over every
axis to a 0-D scalar.

parameters.name: keepdim
parameters.description:
Retain the reduced axes as size-1 dimensions.  Default

returns.description: Minima along `dim`.

see_also.name: lucid.min
see_also.description: returns `(values, indices)` for a single axis.

members.name: aminmax
members.summary: Compute the minimum and maximum of `input`.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description:
Dimension along which to compute minimum and maximum. When `None`
(default), reduces over the entire tensor.

parameters.name: keepdim
parameters.description: If `True`, retains the reduced dimensions with size 1.

returns.description: Named pair `(min, max)` with `.min` and `.max` attributes.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> out = lucid.aminmax(lucid.tensor([3.0, -1.0, 4.0]))
>>> (out.min.item(), out.max.item())
(-1.0, 4.0)

members.name: angle
members.summary: Phase angle (argument) of each element.
members.extended:
Computes the polar-coordinate angle of each complex element:
$\arg(z) = \arctan2(\Im(z), \Re(z))$, in radians on the
interval $[-\pi, \pi]$.  A real element is a complex number on
the real axis: its angle is $\pi$ when it is negative and 0
otherwise, and NaN stays NaN.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Complex or real tensor.  A bool or integer one is taken at the
default floating dtype.

returns.description:
Real tensor with the same shape as `input`: `float32` for
`complex64`, `float64` for `complex128`, a real input's own
floating dtype.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> z = lucid.tensor([1+0j, 1+1j, 0+1j, -1+0j])
>>> lucid.angle(z)
tensor([0., 0.7854, 1.571, 3.142])
>>> lucid.angle(lucid.tensor([-2, 3]))
tensor([3.142, 0.])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out}_i = \arg(z_i) = \arctan2(\Im(z_i), \Re(z_i))
$$

Uses quadrant-correct `lucid.atan2` internally — unlike a naive
`arctan(imag / real)`, this returns the proper four-quadrant angle.
Zero complex inputs yield 0.0 (not NaN).

members.name: arccosh
members.summary: Inverse hyperbolic cosine.
members.extended:
Verbose alias of `acosh`.  Computes the principal branch
$\operatorname{arccosh}(x) = \log\!\bigl(x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\bigr)$,
defined for real $x \geq 1$.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Input tensor; element-wise values must satisfy $x \geq 1$
for a real result.

returns.description: Element-wise inverse hyperbolic cosine, same shape as `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 10.0])
>>> lucid.arccosh(x)
tensor([0., 1.317, 2.993])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\operatorname{arccosh}(x) =
\log\!\bigl(x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\bigr), \qquad x \geq 1.
$$

Inputs with $x < 1$ produce NaN through the real `sqrt`
branch.  The derivative is $1 / \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}$, singular
at $x = 1$.  Both `arccosh` and `acosh` refer to the
same composite; either spelling may be used for parity with NumPy
or reference-framework code.

members.name: arcsinh
members.summary: Inverse hyperbolic sine.
members.extended:
Verbose alias of `asinh`.  Computes
$\operatorname{arcsinh}(x) = \log\!\bigl(x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}\bigr)$,
defined for all real `input`.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor; domain is all of $\mathbb{R}$.

returns.description: Element-wise inverse hyperbolic sine, same shape as `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
>>> lucid.arcsinh(x)
tensor([-0.8814, 0., 0.8814])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\operatorname{arcsinh}(x) =
\log\!\bigl(x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}\bigr).
$$

Odd function: $\operatorname{arcsinh}(-x) = -\operatorname{arcsinh}(x)$.
Derivative is $1 / \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$.  Both `arcsinh` and
`asinh` refer to the same composite.

members.name: arctan2
members.summary: Quadrant-correct two-argument arctangent.
members.extended:
Verbose alias of `lucid.atan2`.  Returns the polar angle
$\theta$ of the point $(x, y)$ in the Cartesian plane,
resolving the correct quadrant from the signs of both arguments.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Ordinate (imaginary / y-coordinate). Must broadcast with `other`.

parameters.name: other
parameters.description: Abscissa (real / x-coordinate). Must broadcast with `input`.

returns.description:
Element-wise angle in radians on $[-\pi, \pi]$, with the
broadcast shape of `input` and `other`.

notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\arctan2(y, x) =
\begin{cases}
    \arctan(y/x),          & x > 0, \\
    \arctan(y/x) + \pi,    & x < 0,\ y \geq 0, \\
    \arctan(y/x) - \pi,    & x < 0,\ y < 0, \\
    +\pi/2,                & x = 0,\ y > 0, \\
    -\pi/2,                & x = 0,\ y < 0, \\
    0,                     & x = 0,\ y = 0.
\end{cases}
$$

The naive $\arctan(y / x)$ collapses both half-planes into
$(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$; `arctan2` instead inspects the sign of
each argument to recover the full $[-\pi, \pi]$ range, which
is essential for converting Cartesian to polar coordinates.

members.name: arctanh
members.summary: Inverse hyperbolic tangent.
members.extended:
Verbose alias of `atanh`.  Computes
$\operatorname{arctanh}(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}\log\!\bigl((1+x)/(1-x)\bigr)$, defined for
$|x| < 1$.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Input tensor; element-wise values must satisfy $|x| < 1$
for a finite real result.

returns.description: Element-wise inverse hyperbolic tangent, same shape as `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([-0.5, 0.0, 0.5])
>>> lucid.arctanh(x)
tensor([-0.5493, 0., 0.5493])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\operatorname{arctanh}(x) =
\tfrac{1}{2}\log\!\Bigl(\tfrac{1 + x}{1 - x}\Bigr),
\qquad |x| < 1.
$$

Boundary values $x = \pm 1$ produce $\pm\infty$;
$|x| > 1$ produces NaN.  Derivative is $1 / (1 - x^{2})$.
Both `arctanh` and `atanh` refer to the same composite.

members.name: argwhere
members.summary: Return the coordinates of every non-zero element in `input`.
members.extended:
Thin alias for `lucid.nonzero` named to match the NumPy /
reference-framework convention.  The output is a synchronisation
point on GPU streams — the kernel can't know how many non-zeros
there are without a device→host count.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Input tensor of any shape and dtype; zero is determined by the
usual truthiness rules (`0` for numeric dtypes, `False` for
bool).

returns.description:
Shape `(N, x.ndim)` `int64` tensor; row `i` lists the
multi-dimensional index of the `i`-th non-zero element in
row-major order.

members.name: asinh
members.summary: Inverse hyperbolic sine.
members.extended: Short-name alias of `arcsinh`. Defined for all real inputs.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor. Domain is all of $\mathbb{R}$.

returns.description: Element-wise inverse hyperbolic sine.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
>>> lucid.asinh(x)
tensor([-0.8814, 0., 0.8814])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\operatorname{asinh}(x) = \log\!\bigl(x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}\bigr).
$$

The function is odd: $\operatorname{asinh}(-x) = -\operatorname{asinh}(x)$.
Derivative is $1 / \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$.

members.name: atanh
members.summary: Inverse hyperbolic tangent.
members.extended:
Short-name alias of `arctanh`. Domain is the open interval
$(-1, 1)$; values at the boundary diverge to $\pm\infty$.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor with values in $|x| < 1$.

returns.description: Element-wise inverse hyperbolic tangent.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([-0.5, 0.0, 0.5])
>>> lucid.atanh(x)
tensor([-0.5493, 0., 0.5493])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\operatorname{atanh}(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,
\log\!\Bigl(\tfrac{1 + x}{1 - x}\Bigr),
\qquad |x| < 1.
$$

Values outside $(-1, 1)$ produce NaN; $x = \pm 1$ produces
$\pm\infty$. The derivative is $1 / (1 - x^{2})$.

members.name: atleast_1d
members.summary: Promote each input to at least 1 dimension.
members.extended:
Scalars (0-D tensors) are reshaped to length-1 vectors; tensors that
already have rank $\geq 1$ pass through unchanged.  Commonly
used as a defensive guard at the top of routines that vectorise over
a leading axis.

parameters.name: *tensors
parameters.description: One or more input tensors of arbitrary rank.

returns.description:
A single tensor when called with one argument, otherwise a tuple
of the promoted tensors in the same order as the inputs.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> s = lucid.tensor(3.0)
>>> v = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0])
>>> a, b = lucid.atleast_1d(s, v)
>>> a.shape, b.shape
((1,), (2,))
notes:
Promotion rule per input `t` with original rank `r`:



$$
\text{shape}'(t) =
\begin{cases}
    (1,),               & r = 0, \\
    \text{shape}(t),    & r \geq 1.
\end{cases}
$$

Mirrors NumPy's `np.atleast_1d`.  Higher-rank `atleast_2d` and
`atleast_3d` variants follow the same pattern with extra leading /
trailing unit axes.

members.name: atleast_2d
members.summary: Promote each input to at least 2 dimensions.
members.extended:
Scalars become shape `(1, 1)`, 1-D tensors gain a leading unit axis
to become `(1, N)`; tensors that already have rank $\geq 2$
pass through unchanged.

parameters.name: *tensors
parameters.description: One or more input tensors of arbitrary rank.

returns.description:
A single tensor when called with one argument, otherwise a tuple
of the promoted tensors in the same order as the inputs.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> v = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
>>> lucid.atleast_2d(v).shape
(1, 3)
notes:
Promotion rule per input `t` with original shape $\mathbf{s}$:



$$
\text{shape}'(t) =
\begin{cases}
    (1, 1),           & \text{ndim}(t) = 0, \\
    (1, N),           & \mathbf{s} = (N,), \\
    \mathbf{s},       & \text{ndim}(t) \geq 2.
\end{cases}
$$

The leading axis insertion (rather than trailing) matches NumPy's
`np.atleast_2d` convention.

members.name: atleast_3d
members.summary: Promote each input to at least 3 dimensions.

parameters.name: *tensors
parameters.description: One or more input tensors of arbitrary rank.

returns.description:
A single tensor when called with one argument, otherwise a tuple
of the promoted tensors in the same order as the inputs.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> v = lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0])
>>> lucid.atleast_3d(v).shape
(1, 2, 1)
notes:
Promotion rule per input `t`:



$$
\text{shape}'(t) =
\begin{cases}
    (1, 1, 1),    & \text{ndim}(t) = 0, \\
    (1, N, 1),    & \text{shape}(t) = (N,), \\
    (M, N, 1),    & \text{shape}(t) = (M, N), \\
    \text{shape}(t), & \text{ndim}(t) \geq 3.
\end{cases}
$$

Note the asymmetric padding: 1-D tensors get both a leading and a
trailing unit axis (so they live in the middle, image-like axis),
while 2-D tensors gain only a trailing channel axis.  This matches
NumPy and is convenient for image-processing code that expects
`(H, W, C)` arrays.

members.name: baddbmm
members.signature: baddbmm(input: Tensor, batch1: Tensor, batch2: Tensor, beta: _float = ..., alpha: _float = ...)
members.summary: Batched GEMM with a batched accumulator.
members.extended:
Computes
$\beta \cdot \text{input} + \alpha \cdot \operatorname{bmm}(\text{batch1}, \text{batch2})$
where the batch axis is preserved (unlike `addbmm` which reduces
it).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Accumulator of shape `(B, M, N)`.

parameters.name: batch1
parameters.description: Batched left matrices of shape `(B, M, K)`.

parameters.name: batch2
parameters.description: Batched right matrices of shape `(B, K, N)`.

parameters.name: beta
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `input`. Defaults to `1.0`.

parameters.name: alpha
parameters.description: Scalar multiplier on `bmm(batch1, batch2)`. Defaults to `1.0`.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(B, M, N)`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> b1 = lucid.ones((3, 2, 4))
>>> b2 = lucid.ones((3, 4, 2))
>>> M = lucid.zeros((3, 2, 2))
>>> lucid.baddbmm(M, b1, b2).shape
(3, 2, 2)
notes:
Per-batch definition:



$$
\text{out}[k] = \beta \cdot \text{input}[k]
+ \alpha \cdot (\text{batch1}[k] \cdot \text{batch2}[k]).
$$

The implementation defers to `lucid.bmm`, which dispatches to
Accelerate-batched GEMM on CPU and MLX on GPU.

members.name: bincount
members.signature: bincount(input: Tensor, weights: Tensor | None = ..., minlength: _int = ...)
members.summary: Count occurrences of each integer value in `input`.
members.extended:
One `scatter_add` into a zero tensor of the output's length.  That
length depends on the largest value, so it costs one read of the
input's minimum and maximum back to the host — the device round trip
every data-dependent output size takes on Metal.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: 1-D tensor of non-negative integers.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description:
1-D, as long as `input`.  When supplied, `output[i]` is the
*sum of weights* for entries with value `i` (rather than the
plain count).  Default `None`.

parameters.name: minlength
parameters.description:
Floor for the output length.  The output has length
`max(input.max() + 1, minlength)`.  Default `0`.

returns.description:
1-D tensor on `input`'s device: `int64` counts without
`weights`; with them, the weights' dtype for `float32` /
`float64` weights and `float64` for any other (`float32` on
Metal, which holds no `float64`).

raises.description: `input` is not an integer tensor.

`input` is not 1-D or holds a negative value, `minlength` is
negative, or `weights` is not 1-D and as long as `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.bincount(lucid.tensor([0, 1, 1, 3]))
tensor([1, 2, 0, 1], dtype=lucid.int64)
>>> lucid.bincount(lucid.tensor([0, 1, 1]), weights=lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]))
tensor([1., 5.])

members.name: block_diag
members.summary: Construct a block-diagonal matrix from a sequence of blocks.
members.extended:
Each input is placed on the diagonal of a larger matrix, with zeros
everywhere off-block. Scalars (0-D) become $1 \times 1$ blocks
and 1-D inputs become $1 \times n$ blocks before stacking.

parameters.name: *tensors
parameters.description:
One or more 0-, 1-, or 2-D tensors to place on the diagonal,
in order from top-left to bottom-right.

returns.description:
2-D block-diagonal matrix of shape
`(sum(h_i), sum(w_i))` where `h_i, w_i` are the (promoted)
block heights and widths.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> A = lucid.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
>>> B = lucid.tensor([[5.]])
>>> lucid.block_diag(A, B)
tensor([[1., 2., 0.], [3., 4., 0.], [0., 0., 5.]])
notes:
For blocks $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$, the result is



$$
\operatorname{blockdiag}(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k) =
\begin{pmatrix}
    A_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
    0 & A_2 & \cdots & 0 \\
    \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
    0 & 0 & \cdots & A_k
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Called with zero arguments, returns an empty `(0, 0)` matrix.

members.name: broadcast_shapes
members.summary: Return the common shape to which `shapes` broadcast.
members.extended:
Applies the standard right-aligned broadcasting rules across zero or
more shape sequences: two dimensions are compatible when they are
equal or one of them is `1`, in which case the output dimension is
their non-unit size (or `0` when an axis has length `0` paired
with `0` or `1`).

parameters.name: *shapes
parameters.description: Zero or more shape tuples or lists of non-negative dimension sizes.

returns.description: The broadcasted shape tuple (`()` when called with no arguments).

raises.description: If any dimension size is negative.

If any two shapes have incompatible non-unit dimensions along the
same right-aligned axis.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.broadcast_shapes((2, 1, 3), (4, 1))
(2, 4, 3)
>>> lucid.broadcast_shapes()
()

members.name: broadcast_tensors
members.summary: Broadcast one or more tensors against each other to a common shape.
members.extended:
Computes the joint shape via `lucid.broadcast_shapes` and returns
a tuple of views produced by `Tensor.broadcast_to`, preserving
autograd tracking on every input tensor.

parameters.name: *tensors
parameters.description: Zero or more tensors whose shapes are broadcast-compatible.

returns.description: Tuple of broadcasted tensor views sharing the common shape.

raises.description: If any argument is not a `Tensor`.
If the input tensor shapes cannot be broadcast together.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.arange(3).reshape(3, 1)
>>> y = lucid.arange(2).reshape(1, 2)
>>> bx, by = lucid.broadcast_tensors(x, y)
>>> bx.shape, by.shape
((3, 2), (3, 2))

members.name: can_cast
members.summary: Predicate: can `from_` be cast to `to` under the promotion rules?
members.extended:
Returns `True` iff `to`'s category is at least `from_`'s
(bool $<$ int $<$ float $<$ complex).  Casts within
a category (both widening and narrowing, e.g. `int8 → int32`,
`int64 → int8`, `float64 → float32`) and casts to a higher
category are permitted; casts to a lower category (e.g.
`float32 → int32`, `complex64 → float32`) are rejected.

parameters.name: from_
parameters.description: Source dtype.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Destination dtype.

returns.description: `True` if the cast is permitted, `False` otherwise.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.can_cast(lucid.int8, lucid.int32)
True
>>> lucid.can_cast(lucid.float64, lucid.float32)
True
>>> lucid.can_cast(lucid.float32, lucid.int32)
False
notes:
With `kind(d)` denoting the category ordering
`bool < int < float < complex`:



$$
\operatorname{can\_cast}(\text{from},\;\text{to})
\;\iff\; \operatorname{kind}(\text{from}) \le \operatorname{kind}(\text{to}).
$$

Contrast with `result_type`, which returns the *target* dtype for
a mixed-type expression rather than a boolean — use `can_cast` for
pre-flight checks, `result_type` for selecting an output dtype.

members.name: cdist
members.signature: cdist(x1: Tensor, x2: Tensor, p: _float = ..., compute_mode: str = ...)
members.summary: Pairwise $L_p$ distance matrix between rows of `x1` and `x2`.
members.extended:
Specialised paths exist for `p` in $\{1, 2, \infty, 0\}$;
other `p` values fall back to the general
$(\sum_k |a_k - b_k|^p)^{1/p}$ formula.  For `p=2` the
numerically stable expansion
$\|a-b\|^2 = \|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2 - 2 a \cdot b^\top$ is used
so large coordinates don't lose precision.

parameters.name: x1
parameters.description: Shape `(..., P, M)`.

parameters.name: x2
parameters.description:
Shape `(..., R, M)`.  Leading batch dimensions are
broadcast-compatible with `x1`.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description:
$L_p$ exponent.  Default `2.0` (Euclidean).  Use
`float("inf")` for Chebyshev, `0.0` for the Hamming-style
non-zero count.

parameters.name: compute_mode
parameters.description:
Controls whether the matrix-multiplication identity is used when
`p == 2.0`.  One of `'use_mm_for_euclid_dist_if_necessary'`
(default), `'use_mm_for_euclid_dist'`, or
`'donot_use_mm_for_euclid_dist'`.

returns.description:
Shape `(..., P, R)`.  Entry $(\ldots, i, j)$ =
$\|x_1[\ldots, i, :] - x_2[\ldots, j, :]\|_p$.

raises.description:
If `x1` or `x2` is not a real floating-point tensor, as the
reference refuses integer, bool and complex inputs — a `TypeError`
and a `RuntimeError`.

members.name: column_stack
members.summary: Stack tensors as columns of a 2-D matrix.
members.extended:
Each 1-D tensor is first promoted to a column vector of shape
`(N, 1)`; tensors with rank `>= 2` are passed through unchanged.
The results are then concatenated along axis 1.

parameters.name: tensors
parameters.description:
Tensors to stack. 1-D tensors are reshaped to column form;
higher-rank tensors must already have matching first-axis size.

returns.description:
2-D tensor formed by concatenating the (possibly promoted)
inputs along axis 1.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> a = lucid.tensor([1., 2., 3.])
>>> b = lucid.tensor([4., 5., 6.])
>>> lucid.column_stack([a, b])
tensor([[1., 4.], [2., 5.], [3., 6.]])
notes:
For all-1-D inputs $v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(k)}$ of length `N`,
the result has shape `(N, k)`:



$$
\text{out}_{ij} = v^{(j)}_i.
$$

For higher-rank inputs, the first dimension is the "row count" along
which axis-1 concatenation happens, matching NumPy semantics.

members.name: combinations
members.summary: All `r`-length combinations of the elements of a 1-D `input`.
members.extended:
The positions of every combination are built on the CPU, then read
from `input` with one `index_select` — differentiable through
`input`, and on its device.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: 1-D source tensor of length $n$.  Raises on higher rank.

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: Combination length.  Default `2`.

parameters.name: with_replacement
parameters.description:
When `True` the output enumerates multisets (an element can
appear multiple times in a single row), giving
$\binom{n + r - 1}{r}$ rows.  Default `False` (strict
combinations, $\binom{n}{r}$ rows).

returns.description:
Shape `(C, r)` where $C$ is the combination count, in
lexicographic order of positions; shape `(0,)` when `r` is 0.
Dtype and device follow `input`.

raises.description: `input` is not 1-D, or `r` is negative.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.combinations(lucid.tensor([1, 2, 3]), r=2)
tensor([[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]], dtype=lucid.int64)

members.name: conj_physical
members.summary: Eagerly materialised complex conjugate.
members.extended:
Some reference frameworks distinguish `conj` (which may set a lazy
"conjugated" flag on the tensor's view) from `conj_physical` (which
always writes a new buffer with the conjugated values).  Lucid does
not carry any lazy conjugation metadata, so both call into the same
engine op — `conj_physical` is provided for API parity and as a
clear signal to readers that the conjugation is materialised.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Input tensor.  Typically `complex64`; for real dtypes the
conjugate is the identity.

returns.description: Element-wise complex conjugate of `input`, same shape and dtype.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> z = lucid.tensor([1+2j, 3-4j])
>>> lucid.conj_physical(z)
tensor([(1.-2.j), (3.+4.j)], dtype=lucid.complex64)
notes:
Mathematical definition for a complex element $z = a + ib$:



$$
\overline{z} = a - i\,b.
$$

Use this spelling when porting code that explicitly depends on the
conjugation being physically present in the storage (e.g. for
interop with external libraries that would otherwise see the lazy
flag).  Functionally identical to `lucid.conj` in Lucid.

members.name: copysign
members.summary: Element-wise sign transplant: magnitudes from `input`, signs from `other`.
members.extended:
Useful for sign-preserving operations that need to preserve a sign
bit independent of an arbitrary magnitude computation.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Magnitude source; result has `|x|` element-wise.

parameters.name: other
parameters.description:
Sign source; result takes the IEEE-754 sign bit of `other`
(broadcastable to the shape of `input`).

returns.description: Broadcast shape of `input` and `other` at their common floating dtype.

members.name: corrcoef
members.summary: Pearson correlation-coefficient matrix.
members.extended:
Composite of `cov` divided by the outer product of the
per-variable standard deviations:

$$
R_{ij} = \frac{C_{ij}}{\sqrt{C_{ii}} \sqrt{C_{jj}}}.
$$

Diagonal entries are `1.0` (up to floating-point); off-diagonal
entries fall in $[-1, 1]$, or inside the unit disc for a complex
`input` (whose covariance is Hermitian, see `cov`).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Shape `(N,)` for a single-variable degenerate case, or
`(N, M)` for `N` variables observed at `M` time points.

returns.description: Shape `(N, N)` Pearson correlation matrix.

see_also.name: cov
see_also.description: raw covariance matrix without the std-normalisation.

members.name: count_nonzero
members.summary: Count non-zero elements along `dim` (or whole tensor when `None`).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Input.  Non-zero is determined by element-wise comparison to
zero (NaN counts as non-zero).

parameters.name: dim
parameters.annotation: int, sequence of int, or None
parameters.description:
Axis or axes to reduce.  `None` (default) reduces the entire
tensor to a 0-D scalar.

returns.description:
`int64` count(s).  Shape mirrors `lucid.sum` over the
same `dim` argument.

notes:
The sum of the bool mask `x != 0`, which is int64 and exact.  It
used to build a float32 `1.0/0.0` mask with `where` and cast the
float sum back — three full-size temporaries and ten times a plain
reduction, from a time the CPU could not sum a bool.

members.name: cov
members.signature: cov(input: Tensor, correction: _int = ..., fweights: Tensor | None = ..., aweights: Tensor | None = ...)
members.summary: Covariance matrix of `input`.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Shape `(N,)` (single-variable degenerate case) or `(N, M)`
— *N* variables observed at *M* time points.

parameters.name: correction
parameters.description:
Bessel correction; the divisor is `max(1, M - correction)`.
Default `1` (unbiased sample covariance); pass `0` for the
biased population covariance.

parameters.name: fweights
parameters.description: 1-D integer tensor of observation repeat counts (length `M`).

parameters.name: aweights
parameters.description: 1-D numeric tensor of relative observation weights (length `M`).

returns.description:
Shape `(N, N)`.  Entry $(i, j)$ =
$\frac{1}{M - \text{correction}}\sum_k (x_{i,k} - \bar x_i)\,\overline{(x_{j,k} - \bar x_j)}$,
so a complex `input` gives a Hermitian matrix with a real diagonal.

notes:
A complex `input` runs on Metal only: the CPU stream has no complex
matrix product.

members.name: cumulative_trapezoid
members.signature: cumulative_trapezoid(y: Tensor, x: Tensor | None = ..., dx: _float | None = ..., dim: _int = ...)
members.summary: Compute the running trapezoidal integral of `y` along `dim`.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Samples to integrate cumulatively.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Grid coordinates along `dim`; mutually exclusive with `dx`.

parameters.name: dx
parameters.description: Constant grid spacing when `x` is omitted.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Axis of cumulative integration (default `-1`).

returns.description: Running integral whose `dim` extent is `y.shape[dim] - 1`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.cumulative_trapezoid(lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 4.0]))
tensor([1.5, 4.5])

members.name: diag_embed
members.summary: Embed the last dimension of `input` as the diagonal of a new matrix.
members.extended:
Inverse of `lucid.diagonal`.  For a 1-D input of length `n`
the result is shape `(n+|offset|, n+|offset|)`.  For batch
inputs the last axis is treated as the diagonal vector and
`dim1` / `dim2` pick which two axes of the *output* carry the
matrix.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Diagonal values.  Any shape; the last axis becomes the
diagonal of each output matrix.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description:
Diagonal offset.  `0` (default) = main diagonal,
positive = above main, negative = below main.  Output size
grows by `|offset|` along each matrix dimension.

parameters.name: dim1
parameters.description: First axis of the output matrix dimensions.  Default `-2`.

parameters.name: dim2
parameters.description: Second axis of the output matrix dimensions.  Default `-1`.

returns.description:
`input.ndim + 1` dims: `input`'s leading dims in order, and two
of size `n + |offset|` at `dim1` (rows) and `dim2` (columns).
Off-diagonal positions are zero.

raises.description: `dim1` or `dim2` outside `[-(input.ndim + 1), input.ndim]`.
`dim1` and `dim2` name the same dim.

members.name: digamma
members.summary: Digamma function $\psi(x) = \frac{d}{dx} \ln \Gamma(x)$.
members.extended:
Implemented as a composite of engine primitives so autograd flows
through naturally, and its gradient is the trigamma function.  For
`x >= 0` the argument is shifted by 8 via
$\psi(x) = \psi(x + 8) - \sum_{k=0}^{7} 1/(x + k)$ and the
asymptotic Bernoulli series is evaluated there; for `x < 0` the
reflection formula $\psi(x) = \psi(1 - x) - \pi \cot(\pi x)$
maps the argument onto the right half.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Real input.  The negative integers and `-inf` are poles and give
NaN; `psi(+0)` is `-inf` and `psi(-0)` is `+inf`.

returns.description: Same shape as `input`.

members.name: divide
members.signature: divide(input: Tensor, other: Tensor | Scalar, rounding_mode: str | None = ...)
members.summary: Element-wise division — `lucid.div` under its longer name.
members.extended:
`rounding_mode=None` is the `/` operator: integer operands are
promoted to a floating dtype.  `"trunc"` rounds the quotient toward
zero and `"floor"` toward negative infinity, keeping an integer dtype.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Numerator.

parameters.name: other
parameters.description: Denominator.

parameters.name: rounding_mode
parameters.description: How the quotient is rounded.  Default `None`: not at all.

returns.description: Element-wise quotient of the broadcast shape of `input` and `other`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.divide(lucid.tensor([6.0, 9.0]), 3.0)
tensor([2., 3.])
>>> lucid.divide(lucid.tensor([7, -7]), 2, rounding_mode="trunc")
tensor([3, -3], dtype=lucid.int64)
notes:
$$
\text{out}_i = \frac{a_i}{b_i}
$$

Division by zero gives $\pm\infty$ (NaN for `0/0`).  The gradients
are $1/b$ and $-a / b^{2}$, and zero for a rounded quotient.

members.name: dsplit
members.summary: Split a tensor along its third (depth) axis.
members.extended:
NumPy-style depth-wise split: cuts the input into pieces along axis 2.
Mirrors `vsplit` (axis 0) and `hsplit` (axis 1).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor with at least 3 dimensions.

parameters.name: indices_or_sections
parameters.description:
- `int`: number of equal-sized splits along axis 2; it must
  divide the axis length.
- `Sequence[int]`: cut indices along axis 2.

returns.description: Sub-tensors whose concatenation along axis 2 reproduces `input`.

raises.description: If `input.ndim < 3`, or a section count does not divide axis 2.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
>>> [s.shape for s in lucid.dsplit(x, 2)]
[(2, 3, 2), (2, 3, 2)]
notes:
For a tensor of shape $(\dots, D, \dots)$ split into `k` pieces
along axis 2, each piece has shape $(\dots, D/k, \dots)$.

members.name: dstack
members.summary: Stack tensors along the third (depth) axis.
members.extended:
Reshapes lower-rank inputs to give them a depth dimension, then
concatenates along axis 2. 0-D scalars become `(1, 1, 1)`, 1-D
vectors of length `N` become `(1, N, 1)`, and 2-D matrices of
shape `(H, W)` become `(H, W, 1)`.

parameters.name: tensors
parameters.description:
Tensors to stack. 0-, 1-, and 2-D inputs are auto-promoted to
3-D as described above; 3-D inputs pass through unchanged.

returns.description:
3-D tensor formed by concatenating the (possibly promoted)
inputs along axis 2.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> a = lucid.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
>>> b = lucid.tensor([[5., 6.], [7., 8.]])
>>> lucid.dstack([a, b]).shape
(2, 2, 2)
notes:
The promotion rules ensure the result is always at least 3-D, which
is useful for stacking colour channels of images: `dstack([R, G, B])`
produces an `(H, W, 3)` tensor from three `(H, W)` planes.

members.name: equal
members.summary: Predicate: do two tensors have the same shape and the same elements?
members.extended:
One Python `bool` for the whole pair, unlike the element-wise
`lucid.eq`.  The shapes must match exactly — no broadcasting —
and the elements are compared at the pair's promoted dtype, so an
integer tensor equals the float tensor holding the same values.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: First tensor.

parameters.name: other
parameters.description: Second tensor.

returns.description:
`True` iff `input.shape == other.shape` and every element pair
compares equal.  `NaN` equals nothing, itself included, and
`-0.0` equals `0.0`.  Two empty tensors of one shape are equal.

raises.description: If either argument is not a `Tensor`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.equal(lucid.tensor([1, 2]), lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0]))
True
>>> lucid.equal(lucid.tensor([1, 2]), lucid.tensor([[1, 2]]))
False
notes: Reading the answer synchronises any pending Metal work on the pair.

members.name: erfc
members.summary: Complementary error function $\text{erfc}(x) = 1 - \text{erf}(x)$.
members.extended:
Computed directly, not as `1 - erf(x)`: past `x ≈ 4` that
difference is a few units of float32's spacing below one, so
`erfc(4)` came back 0 where the answer is 1.54e-8 — and every tail
probability built on it inherited the zero.  The form used is the
Chebyshev fit from Numerical Recipes (`erfcc`), whose relative error
stays below 1.2e-7 for every `input`, carried to negative `input` by
$\text{erfc}(-x) = 2 - \text{erfc}(x)$.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Real-valued input; a bool or integer one is taken at the default float.

returns.description: Same shape as `input`, values in $[0, 2]$.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> abs(lucid.erfc(lucid.tensor(4.0)).item() - 1.5417e-08) < 1e-12
True

members.name: expm1
members.summary: Element-wise $e^{x} - 1$.
members.extended:
Computes the exponential-minus-one function to full relative precision,
including for $|x| \ll 1$, where `exp(x) - 1` cancels: in
float32 that naive form returned `1.19e-7` for `x = 1e-7` (19% off)
and `0` below it.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor. Any floating-point dtype.

returns.description: Element-wise $e^{x} - 1$.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
>>> lucid.expm1(x)
tensor([0., 1.718, 6.389])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out}_i = e^{x_i} - 1.
$$

The function is useful in probability and finance where $x$ is
a small log-difference, since `log(1 + y) = expm1⁻¹(y)` and the pair
avoids subtractive cancellation when chained.

members.name: float_power
members.signature: float_power(input: Tensor | Scalar, exponent: Tensor | Scalar)
members.summary: Element-wise power that always promotes operands to `float64`.
members.extended:
Unlike the regular `lucid.pow`, `float_power` upcasts both
operands to `float64` before exponentiation, so that negative bases
raised to non-integer powers and very large exponents behave
consistently without integer overflow or domain errors.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Base.

parameters.name: exponent
parameters.description: Exponent.

returns.description: Element-wise `x ** y` evaluated in `float64`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([2, 3], dtype=lucid.int32)
>>> lucid.float_power(x, 0.5).dtype
lucid.float64
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out}_i = x_i^{y_i}.
$$

Promotion is mandatory — even integer inputs are cast to `float64`.
The result is always `float64` regardless of input dtype.

members.name: frexp
members.summary:
Decompose `input` into mantissa `m` and exponent `e` such that
`input = m * 2**e` with `|m|` in `[0.5, 1)` (or `m == 0`).
members.extended:
Returns a `(mantissa, exponent)` tuple.  Exponent dtype is int32.
Non-finite inputs and signed zero propagate verbatim:
`NaN -> (NaN, 0)`, `±inf -> (±inf, 0)`, `±0.0 -> (±0.0, 0)`.
Exact on every device, subnormal inputs included.  The mantissa is
differentiable, `dm / dinput = 2**-e` (a subnormal one flushes on
Metal); the exponent is not.

members.name: gcd
members.summary: Element-wise greatest common divisor for integer tensors.
members.extended:
Falls through to Python's `math.gcd` per element — the engine
has no native GCD kernel and this path is for low-rate utility use
(e.g. shape arithmetic), not hot-loop computation.  Non-differentiable.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description:
Tensors whose common dtype is an integer one — an integer tensor
beside a bool one promotes to the integer — broadcastable against
each other.  A 0-d CPU tensor follows the other operand's device.

parameters.name: other
parameters.description:
Tensors whose common dtype is an integer one — an integer tensor
beside a bool one promotes to the integer — broadcastable against
each other.  A 0-d CPU tensor follows the other operand's device.

returns.description:
The broadcast shape at the operands' common dtype, on their common
device.  Each element is `math.gcd(input_i, other_i)` wrapped to
that dtype, as the reference's kernel wraps: non-negative except
`gcd(-2**63, 0)` in int64, which wraps back to `-2**63`.

raises.description:
If either operand is not a tensor (a Python number is refused, as
the reference refuses it), or the operands meet at a float or bool
dtype.
If the operands are on two devices and neither is a 0-d CPU tensor.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.gcd(lucid.tensor([12, 18]), lucid.tensor([8])).tolist()
[4, 2]

members.name: ger
members.summary: Outer product of two 1-D tensors.
members.extended:
Forwards to `lucid.linalg.outer`. Provided under the legacy BLAS
name (`ger` = "general rank-one update") for API parity.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: 1-D tensor of length `M`.

parameters.name: vec2
parameters.description: 1-D tensor of length `N`.

returns.description: 2-D tensor of shape `(M, N)` holding the outer product.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> u = lucid.tensor([1., 2., 3.])
>>> v = lucid.tensor([4., 5.])
>>> lucid.ger(u, v)
tensor([[4., 5.], [8., 10.], [12., 15.]])

Mathematical definition:



$$
\text{out}_{ij} = \text{vec1}_i \cdot \text{vec2}_j.
$$

The result is always rank-1 (in the linear-algebra sense). Use
`addr` to perform a rank-1 update in place of an accumulator.

parameters.description: Number of samples; `>= 0`.

members.name: heaviside
members.summary: Heaviside step function with a user-selectable value at $x = 0$.
members.extended:
Produces `0` for negative inputs and `1` for positive inputs; the
value at exactly zero is taken from `values` (typically `0`,
`0.5`, or `1` depending on convention).

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description:
Value(s) used wherever `x == 0`. If a scalar, it is broadcast to
the shape of `input`; if a tensor, it must broadcast against `input`.

returns.description: Element-wise Heaviside step.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.tensor([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0])
>>> lucid.heaviside(x, 0.5)
tensor([0., 0.5, 1.])
notes:
Mathematical definition:



$$
H(x_i) =
\begin{cases}
    0,            & x_i < 0, \\
    \text{values}_i, & x_i = 0, \\
    1,            & x_i > 0.
\end{cases}
$$

The gradient is zero almost everywhere — the derivative is a Dirac
delta in the distributional sense, which autograd does not propagate.

members.name: histogram
members.signature: histogram(input: Tensor, bins: _int | Sequence[_float] | Tensor = ..., range: tuple[_float, _float] | None = ..., weight: Tensor | None = ..., density: _bool = ...)
members.summary: Compute a 1-D histogram of `input` values.
members.extended:
Everything happens on `input`'s device, without reading a value back
to the host: the range, when not given, is the input's extremes as
tensors; each value's bin is its position on the uniform grid,
corrected against the edges themselves, or a `searchsorted` over
explicit edges; and the bins fill with one `scatter_add`.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Values to bin.  Flattened internally — shape doesn't matter.

parameters.name: bins
parameters.annotation: int, sequence of float or Tensor
parameters.description:
When an int, the number of equal-width bins (default `100`).
Otherwise the increasing bin edges (length `bins_n + 1`).

parameters.name: range
parameters.description:
`(lo, hi)`.  Values outside the range are dropped.  Ignored
when `bins` gives the edges.  `None` (default) →
`(input.min(), input.max())`.  A range of zero width is widened
to `(lo - 0.5, hi + 0.5)`.

parameters.name: density
parameters.description:
When `True` divide by total count × bin width to yield a
probability density that integrates to 1.  Default `False`.

parameters.name: weight
parameters.description:
As many elements as `input`.  When supplied, sums weights per
bin rather than counting.  Default `None`.

returns.description:
`(hist, bin_edges)`, both in `input`'s floating dtype (the
default float dtype for an integer `input`) and on its device.
`hist` holds counts, weight sums or densities; `bin_edges` has
length `bins + 1`.  Every bin is half-open but the last, which
holds its right edge.  When the range comes from an `input`
holding a NaN or an infinity, `hist` is all NaN — the reference
refuses there, which would take a read back to the host.

raises.description:
`bins` is not positive or its edges are fewer than two, the
given `range` is not finite or its `lo` exceeds its `hi`, or
`weight` has another number of elements than `input`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> hist, edges = lucid.histogram(lucid.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 4.0]), bins=4)
>>> hist
tensor([2., 1., 0., 1.])
>>> edges
tensor([1., 1.75, 2.5, 3.25, 4.])

members.name: hsplit
members.summary: Split a tensor horizontally (along axis 1 for rank $\geq 2$).
members.extended:
NumPy-style horizontal split: cuts the input column-wise along axis 1
for tensors of rank $\geq 2$.  For 1-D inputs the axis collapses
to 0, since there is only one dimension available.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Input tensor.  At least 1-D.

parameters.name: indices_or_sections
parameters.description:
- `int`: number of equal-sized splits; it must divide the axis
  length (`tensor_split` takes one that does not).
- `Sequence[int]`: cut indices along the split axis (axis 1
  for rank $\geq 2$, axis 0 for 1-D).

returns.description:
Sub-tensors whose concatenation along the split axis reproduces
`input`.

raises.description: If `input` is 0-d, or a section count does not divide the axis.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> x = lucid.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
>>> [s.shape for s in lucid.hsplit(x, 2)]
[(3, 2), (3, 2)]
>>> v = lucid.arange(6)
>>> [s.shape for s in lucid.hsplit(v, 3)]
[(2,), (2,), (2,)]
notes:
Companion to `vsplit` (axis 0) and `dsplit` (axis 2).
The axis-selection rule



$$
\text{axis} =
\begin{cases}
    0, & \text{ndim}(x) = 1, \\
    1, & \text{ndim}(x) \geq 2,
\end{cases}
$$

matches NumPy's convention so that 1-D inputs behave intuitively
rather than raising on the missing column axis.

members.name: i0
members.summary: Modified Bessel function of the first kind, order 0: $I_0(x)$.
members.extended:
Composite implementation via the Abramowitz & Stegun polynomial
approximation (Table 9.8.1):

* `|x| <= 3.75` — polynomial series in $(x / 3.75)^2$.
* `|x| >  3.75` — polynomial series in $3.75 / |x|$, multiplied
  by $e^{|x|} / \sqrt{|x|}$ to recover the exponential growth.

Each branch runs on `input` clamped into its own interval, so the one
`where` does not pick contributes no `nan` to the gradient.

A `float64` input takes the Cephes double-precision series instead.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Real input.

returns.description: $I_0(x)$ element-wise; always positive.

read as the key `Tensor.__setitem__` reads, by the same owner

`input`, or a bool mask covering as many dims as it has.

parameters.description:
Values of `input`'s dtype, broadcastable to the shape

>>> mask = lucid.tensor([False, False, True, True])
